Abstract

The molecular gas content of normal galaxies at z>4z>4 is poorly constrained, because the commonly used molecular gas tracers become hard to detect at these redshifts. We use the [C ii] 158 μ\mum luminosity, recently proposed as a molecular gas tracer, to estimate the molecular gas content in a large sample of main-sequence star-forming galaxies at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9, with a median stellar mass of 109.7​M⊙10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}, drawn from the ALMA Large Program to INvestigate [C ii] at Early times (ALPINE) survey. The good agreement between molecular gas masses derived from [C ii] luminosities, dynamical masses, and rest-frame 850 μ\mum luminosities, extrapolated from the rest-frame 158 μ\mum continuum, supports [C ii] as a reliable tracer of molecular gas in our sample. We find a continuous decline of the molecular gas depletion timescale from z=0z=0 to z=5.9z=5.9, which reaches a mean value of (4.6±0.8)×108(4.6\pm 0.8)\times 10^{8} yr at z∼5.5z\sim 5.5, only a factor of 2−32-3 shorter than in present-day galaxies. This suggests a mild enhancement of star formation efficiency toward high redshifts, unless the molecular gas fraction significantly increases. Our estimates show that the rise in molecular gas fraction as reported previously, flattens off above z∼3.7z\sim 3.7 to achieve a mean value of 63%±3%63\%\pm 3\% over z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9. This redshift evolution of the gas fraction is in line with the one of the specific star formation rate. We use multi-epoch abundance matching to follow the gas fraction evolution over cosmic time of progenitors of z=0z=0 Milky Way-like galaxies in ∼1013​M⊙\sim 10^{13}\penalty\ M_{\odot} halos and of more massive z=0z=0 galaxies in ∼1014​M⊙\sim 10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} halos. Interestingly, the former progenitors show a monotonic decrease of the gas fraction with cosmic time, while the latter show a constant gas fraction from z=5.9z=5.9 to z∼2z\sim 2 and a steep decrease at z≲2z\lesssim 2. We discuss three possible effects, namely outflows, halt of gas supplying, and over-efficient star formation, which may jointly contribute to the gas fraction plateau of the latter massive galaxies.

Key Words.
galaxies: evolution – galaxies: high-redshift – galaxies: ISM – ISM: molecules

1 Introduction

Since cold molecular hydrogen, H2, is the fuel for star formation, it is necessary to probe the molecular gas content of galaxies with cosmic time to understand their stellar assembly. With an increasing number of normal star-forming galaxies (SFGs) having measurements of their cold molecular gas mass (MmolgasM_{\rm molgas}), we are starting to bring to light the significant role that molecular gas plays in the evolution of these galaxies, which contribute to about 90% of the cosmic star formation rate (SFR) density. They are found to follow the star-forming main-sequence (MS), a tight relation between stellar mass (MstarsM_{\rm stars}) and SFR, which evolves with redshift and has a dispersion of about ±0.3\pm 0.3 dex (Rodighiero et al., 2011; Speagle et al., 2014; Whitaker et al., 2014; Tasca et al., 2015; Faisst et al., 2016, e.g.,). The redshift evolution of the MS is such that, at a given MstarsM_{\rm stars}, high-redshift galaxies form more stars per unit time than low-redshift galaxies, resulting in an increase of their specific star formation rate (sSFR=SFR/Mstars{\rm sSFR=SFR}/M_{\rm stars}) with redshift. It is now well established that, up to z∼2.5z\sim 2.5, the sSFR increase is linked to the observed rise of the molecular gas content of galaxies with redshift (Saintonge et al., 2013; Genzel et al., 2015; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2017; Tacconi et al., 2018; Tacconi et al., 2020; Decarli et al., 2019, e.g.,). Likewise, the location of a galaxy in the SFR–MstarsM_{\rm stars} plane is primarily governed by its supply (mass) of molecular gas and to some extent also its star formation efficiency (SFE=SFR/Mmolgas{\rm SFE=SFR}/M_{\rm molgas}) (Magdis et al., 2012; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Genzel et al., 2015; Silverman et al., 2015; Silverman et al., 2018; Scoville et al., 2016; Tacconi et al., 2020, e.g.,).

To explain the high SFR and MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} of SFGs in the early Universe, it has been proposed that they must be sustained with cold gas accreted from the cosmic web (Keres̆ et al., 2005; Dekel et al., 2009, e.g.,). In this context, the MS may be interpreted in terms of a “bathtub” model, in which MS galaxies lie in a quasi-steady state equilibrium whereby star formation is regulated by the available gas reservoir, and whose content is replenished through pristine gas accretion flows and, eventually, diminished by the amount of material galaxies returned to the intergalactic medium through outflows (Bouché et al., 2010; Davé et al., 2011; Davé et al., 2012; Lilly et al., 2013; Dekel & Mandelker, 2014, e.g.,). Beside the average growth of SFGs along the MS, simulations suggest SFGs oscillate up and down in sSFR across the MS dispersion, owing to feedback effects altering the gas accretion rates, internal gas transport, and compaction events (Tacchella et al., 2016; Orr et al., 2019). The bathtub model agrees with most of the scaling relations observed for MS SFGs, such as the Kennicutt-Schmidt star-formation law (Kennicutt, 1998b; Tacconi et al., 2013) and the mass-metallicity relation (Erb et al., 2006; Maiolino et al., 2008; Mannucci et al., 2010; Ginolfi et al., 2019, e.g.,), and with the dynamically more turbulent galactic disks at high-redshift (Förster Schreiber et al., 2009; Wisnioski et al., 2015; Molina et al., 2017; Girard et al., 2018, e.g.,).

While H2 is the most abundant molecule in the Universe, it is nevertheless difficult to detect in cold media, because it features no emission lines with excitation temperatures below 100 K. Fortunately, cold molecular gas is not pure H2, but contains heavier elements like carbon and oxygen, and is mixed with dust grains. Thus, three indirect cold H2 tracers are commonly used to estimate the H2 content of high-redshift galaxies: the CO molecule rotational transitions (Bolatto et al., 2013, and references therein); the dust mass inferred from the fit of the thermal far-infrared (FIR) dust spectral energy distribution (SED) (Leroy et al., 2011; Magdis et al., 2011; Santini et al., 2014; Béthermin et al., 2015; Kaasinen et al., 2019, e.g.,); and the cold dust continuum emission measured in the Rayleigh-Jeans tail regime of the FIR SED (Scoville et al., 2014; Scoville et al., 2016; Scoville et al., 2017, e.g.,). The Plateau de Bure interferometer – now the Northern Extended Millimeter Array (NOEMA) – and the Atacama Large Millimeter/sub-millimeter Array (ALMA) have largely contributed to the census of MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} in MS SFGs over the peak of the cosmic star formation from z=0z=0 to z∼3.5z\sim 3.5 (Daddi et al., 2010; Magnelli et al., 2012; Tacconi et al., 2013; Tacconi et al., 2018; Saintonge et al., 2013; Saintonge et al., 2017; Santini et al., 2014; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Schinnerer et al., 2016; Decarli et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019b, e.g.,). At higher redshifts, both CO and dust become harder to detect, because of (i) the surface brightness dimming as (1+z)4(1+z)^{4}, (ii) the lower metallicities expected in distant galaxies making CO dark and dust rare, and (iii) the ALMA bands only covering high (J≥5J\geq 5) CO transitions at z>4.5z>4.5, which requires the knowledge of the CO excitation state and gas density to determine the total MmolgasM_{\rm molgas}. Therefore, only two MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} estimates derived from CO luminosity measurements were reported in MS SFGs at z>5.5z>5.5 to date (D’Odorico et al., 2018; Pavesi et al., 2019). And the dozens of MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} measurements derived from FIR dust continuum for MS SFGs at z>4z>4 (Scoville et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2019b) are largely biased toward massive galaxies with Mstars≳1011.5​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\gtrsim 10^{11.5}\penalty\ M_{\odot} (and hence high SFRs).

Clearly, the MS is not yet adequately covered at these high redshifts (Liu et al., 2019b, see the right panel of Fig. 4 of): molecular gas masses of MS SFGs at z>4z>4, for a large parameter space of MstarsM_{\rm stars} and SFR, still need to be accessed to establish how gas reservoirs and gas consumption timescales change as a function of at least three fundamental parameters, namely the cosmic time, MstarsM_{\rm stars}, and SFR. The study of the molecular gas content of galaxies over 4<z<64<z<6 is all the more important as such redshift range corresponds to the key evolutionary phase in the early life of galaxies, between their primordial and mature phase, with many fundamental properties of present-day galaxies being established (Ribeiro et al., 2016; Feldmann, 2015). During this early phase, galaxies are known to double their MstarsM_{\rm stars} at 5 to 10 times higher rates than at later cosmic times (Faisst et al., 2016; Davidzon et al., 2018), which may require very efficient star formation and/or considerable supply of molecular gas.

The C+ radiation, considered as an important coolant of the neutral interstellar medium (ISM), accessible through the [C ii] line at 158 μ\mum (Carilli & Walter, 2013, one of the strongest line in the FIR spectra; see) and shown to correlate with the total SFR in galaxies (De Looze et al., 2011; De Looze et al., 2014; Schaerer et al., 2020, e.g.,), has been found to be a good tracer of molecular gas, first at 0.03<z<0.20.03<z<0.2 by Hughes et al. (2017a) and recently over 0<z<60<z<6 by Zanella et al. (2018). Such a correlation between [C ii] luminosity (LCIIL_{\rm CII}) and MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} can be exploited to overcome the observational challenge of detecting CO or FIR dust emission in very high-redshift normal SFGs. In this context, our recently completed ALMA Large Program to INvestigate [C ii] at Early times (Le Fèvre et al., 2020; Béthermin et al., 2020; Faisst et al., 2020, ALPINE;) delivers the first sample of 75 [C ii] emission detections and 43 upper limits obtained for a representative population of ultraviolet (UV) selected MS SFGs at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 with SFR≳10​M⊙​yr−1{\rm SFR}\gtrsim 10\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ \rm yr^{-1} and Mstars=108.4−1011​M⊙M_{\rm stars}=10^{8.4}-10^{11}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. Relying on the Zanella et al. (2018) correlation, we use the ALPINE data to provide the first set of molecular gas mass estimates for MS SFGs at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9.

In Sect. 2 we summarise the ALPINE survey, the physical properties of galaxies in our survey, and the ALMA observations. Measurements of molecular gas masses obtained using [C ii] luminosity are presented in Sect. 3, together with specific tests of [C ii] as a reliable molecular gas tracer for the ALPINE galaxies. In Sect. 4 we describe the comparison sample, which includes lower redshift MS SFGs with molecular gas masses determined from CO luminosities. We argue why CO-detected MS galaxies represent a better comparison sample with respect to FIR continuum-detected SFGs having typically large MstarsM_{\rm stars}. In Sect. 5 we discuss the inferred molecular gas depletion timescales and the molecular gas fractions, which we compare to those of lower redshift CO-detected galaxies. The evolution of the molecular gas fraction over cosmic time is described in Sect. 5.3. We use the multi-epoch abundance matching predictions to connect the progenitors at high redshifts with their descendants at z=0z=0. Our main results are summarised in Sect. 6.

Throughout the paper, we assume the Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology with Ωm=0.3\Omega_{m}=0.3, ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7 and H0=70​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=70\penalty\ \rm km\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ Mpc^{-1}, and we adopt the Chabrier (2003) initial mass function.

2 Observations and physical properties of ALPINE galaxies

The 118 targeted galaxies from the ALPINE survey (Le Fèvre et al. 2020 – survey paper; Béthermin et al. 2020 – data reduction paper; Faisst et al. 2020 – ancillary data paper) are UV-selected galaxies from the COSMic evOlution Survey (Scoville et al., 2007, COSMOS, 105 galaxies;) and the Extended Chandra Deep Field South survey (Giacconi et al., 2002, ECDFS, 13 galaxies;). All galaxies have optical spectroscopy, ensuring reliable rest-frame UV spectroscopic redshift measurements, and benefit from multi-wavelength ground- and space-based imaging from UV to IR.

The detailed description of the ancillary spectra and photometric data can be found in Faisst et al. (2020), together with the redshift measurements and the SED fits. The derived MstarsM_{\rm stars} and SFR of ALPINE galaxies are in the range of Mstars=108.4−1011​M⊙M_{\rm stars}=10^{8.4}-10^{11}\penalty\ M_{\odot} and SFRSED=3−630​M⊙​yr−1{\rm SFR}_{\rm SED}=3-630\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ \rm yr^{-1}, respectively, following the expected MS at z∼5z\sim 5. There is a good agreement between SFRSED{\rm SFR}_{\rm SED} and SFRUV+IR\rm SFR_{\rm UV+IR}, as shown by Schaerer et al. (2020). The latter corresponds to the sum of SFRUV\rm SFR_{UV}, measured from the UV luminosity at 1500 Å rest-frame (uncorrected for dust attenuation), and SFRIR\rm SFR_{IR}, measured from the rest-frame 158 μ\mum dust continuum emission flux and the FIR SED template of Béthermin et al. (2017) to infer the total IR luminosity (LIRL_{\rm IR}) integrated between 8 μ\mum and 1000 μ\mum as described in Béthermin et al. (2020). Throughout the paper, we adopt MstarsM_{\rm stars} listed in Table A1 of Faisst et al. (2020), based on photometry that includes the Spitzer IR imaging, and SFRUV+IR\rm SFR_{UV+IR} derived from the UV magnitudes listed in Table A1 of Faisst et al. (2020) and LIRL_{\rm IR} given in Table B1 of Béthermin et al. (2020). For galaxies undetected in the FIR dust continuum (95 ALPINE galaxies), we consider only SFRUV\rm SFR_{UV} throughout the paper. Schaerer et al. (2020) discuss in detail the possible amount of SFRIR\rm SFR_{IR}, the dust-obscured star formation rate, in these 95 ALPINE galaxies and find that their total SFR can be underestimated by a factor of 1.6, on average, according to the average empirically-calibrated relation between infrared excess (IRX=LIR/LUV{\rm IRX}=L_{\rm IR}/L_{\rm UV}) and UV spectral slope (β\beta; fλ∝λβf_{\lambda}\propto\lambda^{\beta}), derived by Fudamoto et al. (2020) for the ALPINE sample from median stacking of individual continuum images in bins of β\beta. For the majority of the 95 ALPINE galaxies, however, SFRIR\rm SFR_{IR} turns out to be small (≲40%\lesssim 40\% of SFRUV\rm SFR_{UV}), since their UV spectral slope is fairly blue. We would like to foreshadow that none of our conclusions change when we take the possible underestimation of the total SFR into account.

The ALMA observations were carried out in band 7 during Cycles 5 and 6, and completed in February 2019. Band 7 (275−373275-373 GHz) covers the [C ii] 158 μ\mum line from z=4.1z=4.1 to z=5.9z=5.9, but to avoid an atmospheric absorption no source was included in the redshift range of z=4.6−5.1z=4.6-5.1. Each target was observed for 15−2515-25 minutes of on-source time, with the phase center positioned at the rest-frame UV position of the target and one spectral window in the lower-frequency sideband tuned to the [C ii] frequency redshifted by the rest-frame UV spectroscopic redshift of that target (Faisst et al., 2020). The other three spectral windows were used for the FIR continuum around 158 μ\mum rest-frame, close to the FIR SED peak. The ALMA visibility calibration, cleaning, and imaging were performed using the Common Astronomy Software Applications package (McMullin et al., 2007, CASA;), as described in detail in Béthermin et al. (2020). The resulting root-mean-square noise (RMS) of the 118 [C ii] data cubes ranges between 0.2​mJy​beam−10.2\penalty\ \rm mJy\penalty\ beam^{-1} and 0.55​mJy​beam−10.55\penalty\ \rm mJy\penalty\ beam^{-1} per 25​km​s−125\penalty\ \rm km\penalty\ s^{-1} channel for an angular resolution varying between 0.72​″0.72\arcsec (minimum minor axis) and 1.6​″1.6\arcsec (maximum major axis). The continuum sensitivity varies with frequency. We reach a mean RMS of 50​μ​Jy​beam−150\penalty\ \mu\rm Jy\penalty\ beam^{-1} for ALPINE galaxies at z=4.4−4.6z=4.4-4.6, and 28​μ​Jy​beam−128\penalty\ \mu\rm Jy\penalty\ beam^{-1} for ALPINE galaxies at z=5.1−5.9z=5.1-5.9. The ALMA dataset leads to robust [C ii] emission detections for 75 ALPINE galaxies and robust FIR dust continuum emission detections for 23 ALPINE galaxies, with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) larger than 3.5 corresponding to 95% purity threshold of both the [C ii] line and FIR continuum (Béthermin et al., 2020). Throughout the paper, we consider the 2​σ2\,\sigma-clipped [C ii] fluxes11 1 The 2​σ2\,\sigma-clipped flux corresponds to the flux integrated within the region around the source defined by the contour level at SNR=2\rm SNR=2 in the moment-zero map. The 2​σ2\,\sigma-clipped fluxes are similar to the 2D-fit fluxes obtained from two-dimensional elliptical Gaussian fits over a 3′′3^{\prime\prime} fitting box around the source (Béthermin et al., 2020, see Fig. 16 in)., and the FIR continuum fluxes derived using the 2D elliptical Gaussian fits. For the 43 ALPINE targets with no [C ii] detections, we consider the “secure” 3​σ3\,\sigma upper limits22 2 The “secure” 3​σ3\,\sigma upper limits on [C ii] fluxes are calculated by adding the 3​σ3\,\sigma RMS of the noise to the highest flux measured in 1′′1^{\prime\prime} around the phase center in visibility-tapered velocity-integrated flux maps (Béthermin et al., 2020). on [C ii] fluxes listed in Table C2 of Béthermin et al. (2020).

At the achieved angular resolutions, with an average circularized beam of 0.9​″0.9\arcsec, corresponding to ∼5.3−6.1\sim 5.3-6.1 kpc at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9, about 2/3 of the ALPINE [C ii]-detected galaxies are moderately spatially resolved in the [C ii] velocity-integrated intensity maps (Béthermin et al., 2020; Le Fèvre et al., 2020; Fujimoto et al., 2020), meaning their intrinsic (total) sizes as seen in [C ii] emission are about the size of the beam, or a significant fraction thereof, as illustrated by the spectacular object studied by Jones et al. (2020). A large diversity of [C ii] emission morphologies is observed, from compact/unresolved objects, objects appearing as very extended (Fujimoto et al., 2020; Ginolfi et al., 2020b), to objects showing double, or more, merger-like components (Jones et al., 2020). From our morpho-kinematic visual classification, described in Le Fèvre et al. (2020), based on the [C ii] emission and velocity field and multi-band optical to IR images, we find signatures of possibly interacting systems for 31 ALPINE [C ii]-detected galaxies, while only 9 ALPINE galaxies are likely rotation-dominated, indicating that the mass assembly through merging process is frequent at these redshifts for MS SFGs. In what follows, we exclude the 31 galaxies classified as mergers to work with a sample of galaxies where robust measurements of their physical properties can be determined, since deblending the [C ii] and dust continuum emissions in closely interacting multi-component systems is difficult with the currently available ALMA data (Béthermin et al., 2020). Therefore, our final sample consists of 87 ALPINE galaxies, of which 44 are detected in [C ii], while 43 only have [C ii] upper limits.

3 Molecular gas mass estimates

3.1 [C ii] as a tracer of cold molecular gas

Zanella et al. (2018) have recently proposed the use of [C ii] emission as a tracer of molecular gas by finding a tight empirical correlation, with a 0.3 dex dispersion, between the [C ii] luminosity and molecular gas mass derived using mainly the CO tracer (Hughes et al., 2017a, see also). This relation seems to hold regardless of the MS or starburst nature of galaxies, redshift (from z=0z=0 to z=6z=6), and metallicity (from 12+log⁡(O/H)=7.912+\log({\rm O/H})=7.9 to 12+log⁡(O/H)=8.812+\log({\rm O/H})=8.8). Zanella et al. (2018) motivate their finding with an explanation of the LCII/LIRL_{\rm CII}/L_{\rm IR} deficit observed in ultra-luminous IR galaxies (ULIRGs) and high-redshift starbursts. Indeed, if LCIIL_{\rm CII} traces MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} (and LIRL_{\rm IR} the SFR), then the [C ii] deficit reflects shorter molecular gas depletion timescales in ULIRGs and distant starbursts, consistently with measurements by Daddi et al. (2010) and Genzel et al. (2010).

From the theoretical point of view, the origin of the emission of [C ii] is complex, because different ISM phases – ionised, neutral, and molecular – are contributing to it. As a result, one needs to establish whether the fraction of [C ii] emission arising from photodissociation regions (Stacey et al., 1991; Malhotra et al., 2001; Cormier et al., 2015; Diaz-Santos et al., 2017, PDRs;), produced by the UV radiation from hot stars heating the outer layers of molecular clouds and associated with both the interface layer of neutral gas as well as ionised gas in the H ii region itself, is dominating (or not dominating) that arising from the CO photodissociation into C and C+ in the cold neutral medium of molecular clouds (Maloney & Black, 1988; Madden et al., 1993; Wolfire et al., 2010; Narayanan & Krumholz, 2017). In the PDR case C+ is rather tracing star formation, while in the CO photodissociation case C+ emission emerges from the molecular phase.

The [C ii] line has raised considerable interest in galaxies at z≳5z\gtrsim 5, leading several numerical simulations to model [C ii] and to suggest that its emission is dominated at level of >60−85>60-85% by molecular clouds more than by diffuse ionised gas (Vallini et al., 2015; Pallottini et al., 2017; Accurso et al., 2017; Olsen et al., 2018). Indeed, CO and [C ii] emission maps of the high-redshift galaxy simulated by Vallini et al. (2018) and Pallottini et al. (2017), respectively, clearly show the same morphology with similar spatial distributions on 30 pc scale. In our Milky Way, dense PDRs and CO-dark H2 gas are also the dominant [C ii] emitters, responsible for ∼55\sim 55% of the total [C ii] emission, while the diffuse ionised gas and diffuse neutral gas contribute to ∼20\sim 20% and ∼25\sim 25%, respectively (Pineda et al. 2014; and see also the simulation predictions from Li et al. 2018). As Zanella et al. (2018) warn, when using [C ii] as a molecular gas tracer one needs to be aware that since the C+ emission might not fully emerge from one single gas phase, the measured [C ii] luminosity might overestimate the luminosity arising from the molecular gas even in high-redshift galaxies. On the other hand, as C+ is emitted only in regions where star formation is taking place, the molecular gas not illuminated by stars would not be detected.

Applying the calibration of Zanella et al. (2018) between [C ii] luminosity and molecular gas mass:

log⁡(LCIIL⊙)=(−1.28±0.21)+(0.98±0.02)​log⁡(MmolgasCIIM⊙)\log\left(\frac{L_{\rm CII}}{L_{\odot}}\right)=(-1.28\pm 0.21)+(0.98\pm 0.02)\log\left(\frac{M^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas}}{M_{\odot}}\right) (1)

to the 44 ALPINE [C ii]-detected non-merger galaxies with log⁡(LCII/L⊙)=7.8−9.2\log(L_{\rm CII}/L_{\odot})=7.8-9.2, in the regime tested by Zanella et al. (2018), we obtain molecular gas masses in the range of log⁡(MmolgasCII/M⊙)=9.2−10.8\log(M^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas}/M_{\odot})=9.2-10.8 for these MS SFGs at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9, as shown by the MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} distribution in Fig. 1. We calculate the error bars on the [C ii]-estimated molecular gas masses by summing in quadrature the relative uncertainty of [C ii] fluxes (Béthermin et al., 2020, see) and the 0.3 dex dispersion of the LCIIL_{\rm CII}–MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} calibration (Zanella et al., 2018).

3.2 Other cold molecular gas mass tracers

In what follows, for a subset of the ALPINE sample we cross-correlate the [C ii]-derived molecular gas mass estimates with molecular gas masses inferred using other molecular gas tracers to check the robustness of [C ii] as the tracer of cold molecular gas in our sample of 4.4<z<5.94.4<z<5.9 MS SFGs.

3.2.1 The IR versus CO luminosity relation

We can use the well established empirical relation between IR luminosity and CO(1–0) luminosity measurements (Daddi et al., 2010; Carilli & Walter, 2013; Sargent et al., 2014; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015) to test if the derived MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} agree with the measured LIRL_{\rm IR} along the expected relation. This relation, which spans almost 5 orders of magnitude in LIRL_{\rm IR} from 109​L⊙10^{9}\penalty\ L_{\odot} to 1013.5​L⊙10^{13.5}\penalty\ L_{\odot}, was found to be valid for a variety of galaxy types from MS galaxies, starbursts to mergers at redshifts between z=0z=0 and z∼5.3z\sim 5.3. In Fig. 2 we show the IR luminosities measured for 11 ALPINE [C ii]-detected non-merger galaxies as a function of the CO(1–0) luminosities inferred from the [C ii] molecular gas masses and a range of CO-to-H2 conversion factors (αCO\alpha_{\rm CO}) from the Milky Way value of 4.36​M⊙​(K​km​s−1​pc2)−14.36\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ \rm(K\penalty\ km\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ pc^{2})^{-1} to the starburst value of 1​M⊙​(K​km​s−1​pc2)−11\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ \rm(K\penalty\ km\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ pc^{2})^{-1} (Bolatto et al., 2013). We find that for the Milky Way CO-to-H2 conversion factor all ALPINE galaxies fall within the 0.38 dex dispersion of the IR luminosity versus CO(1–0) luminosity relation, log⁡(LIR/L⊙)=(1.17±0.03)​log⁡(LCO⁡(1−0)′/L⊙)+(0.28±0.23)\log(L_{\rm IR}/L_{\odot})=(1.17\pm 0.03)\log(L^{\prime}_{\rm CO(1-0)}/L_{\odot})+(0.28\pm 0.23), calibrated by Dessauges-Zavadsky et al. (2015), but comparable to Carilli & Walter (2013).

3.2.2 The dust continuum molecular gas masses

At long-wavelengths in the Rayleigh-Jeans tail regime (λrest≳250\lambda_{\rm rest}\gtrsim 250 μ\mum), the thermal dust emission is optically thin and the observed flux density is directly dependent on the mass of dust, the dust opacity coefficient, and the mean temperature of dust contributing to the emission at these wavelengths (Scoville et al., 2016). By assuming that the molecular gas dominates the overall gas budget (the atomic and ionised gas content being negligible) and fixing a dust-to-gas mass ratio, we can then recover the molecular gas mass from the derived dust mass. The rest-frame 850 μ\mum luminosity (L850​μ​mL_{850\mu\rm m}) was found to exhibit a tight correlation with the ISM molecular gas mass and is now frequently used as a molecular gas tracer (Scoville et al., 2014; Scoville et al., 2016; Scoville et al., 2017; Hughes et al., 2017b; Privon et al., 2018; Kaasinen et al., 2019). The difficulty remains in deriving L850​μ​mL_{850\mu\rm m} from often a single-band FIR continuum measurement, since this requires us to assume a dust opacity coefficient and a mean dust temperature, or to know the FIR SED characteristic of the studied galaxies.

Béthermin et al. (2020) constructed the mean stacked FIR SEDs specific to ALPINE galaxy analogues, following the same prescriptions as in Béthermin et al. (2015), but using the more recent COSMOS catalogue of Davidzon et al. (2017) and deep SCUBA2 data at 850 μ\mum from Casey et al. (2013). Moreover, the targets to be stacked were selected with properties analogous to the ones of the ALPINE galaxies: SFR≳10​M⊙​yr−1{\rm SFR}\gtrsim 10\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ \rm yr^{-1}, and redshift bins of 4<z<54<z<5 and 5<z<65<z<6. The resulting SEDs are best-fit by the Béthermin et al. (2017) SED template, but both the Schreiber et al. (2018) SED template and a modified blackbody (MBB) with dust opacity spectral index fixed to β=1.8\beta=1.8 and luminosity-weighted dust temperature of 41±141\pm 1 K at z<5z<5 and 43±543\pm 5 K at z>5z>5 provide a good fit (Béthermin et al., 2020, χ2<4\chi^{2}<4 for 4 degrees of freedom; see Fig. 9 in).

We adopt the Béthermin et al. (2017) FIR SED template to estimate L850​μ​mL_{850\mu\rm m} of the 11 ALPINE non-merger galaxies with FIR continuum detections by scaling the measured monochromatic rest-frame 158 μ\mum luminosity by the ratio between the SED-predicted luminosities at 850 μ\mum and 158 μ\mum. Using then the calibration of Kaasinen et al. (2019)33 3 The calibration of Kaasinen et al. (2019) is comparable to the calibration of Scoville et al. (2016) with a constant α850​μ​m=L850​μ​m/Mmolgas850​μ​m=(6.7±1.7)×1019​erg​s−1​Hz−1​M⊙−1\alpha_{850\mu{\rm m}}=L_{\rm 850\mu\rm m}/M^{850\mu\rm m}_{\rm molgas}=(6.7\pm 1.7)\times 10^{19}\penalty\ {\rm erg\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ Hz^{-1}}\penalty\ M_{\odot}^{-1}, although it shows some deviations at L850​μ​m≲5×1030​erg​s−1​Hz−1L_{\rm 850\mu\rm m}\lesssim 5\times 10^{30}\penalty\ \rm erg\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ Hz^{-1}, but which remains well within the scatter of data used to establish the calibrations.:

These values, although relying on multiple assumptions (e.g., the SED template), are independent measurements to be compared with MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} inferred from the [C ii] luminosity. The comparison is shown in Fig. 3. Within 1−2​σ1-2\,\sigma uncertainty of 0.3−0.60.3-0.6 dex, we find an agreement between these two measurements, although there is some trend for a systematic overestimate of MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} with respect to Mmolgas850​μ​mM^{850\mu\rm m}_{\rm molgas} by 0.3 dex, on average. A similar offset is observed for the Schreiber et al. (2018) SED template and the MBB. On the other hand, when considering the calibration of Groves et al. (2015, Table 5 and > log ( / M stars M ⊙ ) 9 ), obtained for local galaxies, between monochromatic luminosity in the Herschel PACS 160 μ\mum band and gas mass, which relies on much fewer assumptions, we find only a marginal overestimate by 0.1 dex of MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} relative to these gas mass estimates (open squares).

The observed MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} overestimate with respect to Mmolgas850​μ​mM^{850\mu\rm m}_{\rm molgas} may be attributed to three possible effects. First, it points to potential contributions from the neutral atomic and ionised phases to the measured [C ii] emission, in addition to the molecular gas phase. Second, it suggests that the calibration of Kaasinen et al. (2019) may not be valid for the ALPINE galaxies at z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5. Remember that the Scoville et al. (2014) method assumes a constant dust-to-gas mass ratio of ∼1:100\sim 1:100, as also supported by Kaasinen et al. (2019). Yet we may expect a lower dust-to-gas mass ratio (∝α850​μ​m\propto\alpha_{850\mu\rm m} in Eq. (2)) for the ALPINE galaxies, since ALPINE galaxies have lower MstarsM_{\rm stars} (with a median of 109.7​M⊙10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}) than SFGs with Mstars>1010.3​M⊙M_{\rm stars}>10^{10.3}\penalty\ M_{\odot} studied by Scoville et al. (2016) and Kaasinen et al. (2019) and are deficient in dust obscured star-formation activity with respect to lower redshift SFGs as found by Fudamoto et al. (2020). To reconcile Mmolgas850​μ​mM^{850\mu\rm m}_{\rm molgas} with MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas}, α850​μ​m\alpha_{850\mu\rm m} would need to be lower by a factor of ∼2\sim 2. Third, it supports that the SED in the Rayleigh-Jeans tail out to 850 μ\mum rest-frame could be dominated by a cold component. When fixing the dust opacity spectral index to β=1.8\beta=1.8 and considering this time a mass-weighted dust temperature of Tdust=25T_{\rm dust}=25 K in the MBB SED parametrization, similarly to Scoville et al. (2016); Scoville et al. (2017), which we use to extrapolate the 158 μ\mum luminosity to the 850 μ\mum luminosity, we obtain comparable gas masses (filled stars in Fig. 3) to MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas}.

3.2.3 The dynamical masses

As discussed in Le Fèvre et al. (2020), 2/3 of the ALPINE [C ii]-detected galaxies are moderately spatially resolved. For a subset of 18 non-merger galaxies with high-SNR (≳5\gtrsim 5) [C ii] detections, Fujimoto et al. (2020) derived their [C ii] sizes by performing exponential-disk profile fits in the visibility plane with UVMULTIFIT (Martí-Vidal et al., 2014). The circularized effective radii (rer_{e}), defined as the square-root of the product of the effective major and minor axes, are adopted as size measurements and are listed in Table 1 of Fujimoto et al. (2020). For the ALPINE galaxies with size measurement, we can derive their dynamical mass under the assumption that the gas potential structure of ALPINE galaxies arises in a virialised spherical system of radius equal to the measured circularized effective radius and with the one-dimensional velocity dispersion (σCII\sigma_{\rm CII}) inferred from the full-width half maximum (FWHMCIIintrinsic\rm FWHM_{\rm CII}^{\rm intrinsic}) of the [C ii] line corrected for final channel spacing44 4 FWHMCIIintrinsic=FWHMCIIobserved​ 2−252\rm FWHM_{\rm CII}^{\rm intrinsic}=\sqrt{\rm FWHM_{\rm CII}^{\rm observed\penalty\ 2}-25^{2}}, where 25​km​s−125\penalty\ \rm km\penalty\ s^{-1} is the spectral resolution that, in our spectral configuration, equals the final channel spacing (ALMA Technical Handbook). We then obtain the velocity dispersion from σCII=FWHMCIIintrinsic/8​ln⁡(2)\sigma_{\rm CII}=\rm FWHM_{\rm CII}^{\rm intrinsic}/\sqrt{8\ln(2)}.:

Mdynvirial​(M⊙)=1.56×106​(σCIIkm​s−1)2​(rekpc),M_{\rm dyn}^{\rm virial}\penalty\ (M_{\odot})=1.56\times 10^{6}\left(\frac{\sigma_{\rm CII}}{{\rm km\penalty\ s^{-1}}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{r_{e}}{{\rm kpc}}\right), (3)

following Eq. (10) in Bothwell et al. (2013). This virialised spherical geometry dynamical mass is 0.13 dex larger than the dynamical mass we would obtain if we assumed a disk-like gas potential distribution for the same source size, the same FWHMCIIintrinsic\rm FWHM_{\rm CII}^{\rm intrinsic}, and a mean inclination angle of the source of ⟨sin⁡i⟩=π/4\langle\sin i\rangle=\pi/4 (Law et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2013; Capak et al., 2015). But, the virial mass has the advantage of avoiding to add the supplementary uncertainty on the source orientation needed in the computation of the dynamical mass for disk geometry. For 5 out of the 9 ALPINE galaxies classified as rotation-dominated systems (Le Fèvre et al., 2020), we obtained robust [C ii] minor and major axis ratio measurements (Fujimoto et al., 2020), which enable us to constrain their disk inclination angle (ii) as i=cos−1⁡(minor/major)i=\cos^{-1}(\rm minor/major). For these 5 galaxies, we also compute their dynamical mass for the disk-like gas potential distribution:

Mdynrotation​(M⊙)=1.16×105​(υcirkm​s−1)​(2​rekpc),M_{\rm dyn}^{\rm rotation}\penalty\ (M_{\odot})=1.16\times 10^{5}\left(\frac{\upsilon_{\rm cir}}{{\rm km\penalty\ s^{-1}}}\right)\left(\frac{2r_{e}}{{\rm kpc}}\right), (4)

where the circular velocity of the gaseous disk is υcir=1.763​σCII/sin⁡(i)\upsilon_{\rm cir}=1.763\sigma_{\rm CII}\,/\sin(i). The corresponding dynamical masses are randomly scattered by up to ±0.25\pm 0.25 dex from virial masses.

Since the relative contribution of dark matter in the internal regions of galaxies (at <(1−2)​re<(1-2)r_{e}) is expected to be low (Barnabè et al. (2012) report a dark matter fraction within 2.2​re2.2r_{e} of at most 0.28−0.10+0.150.28^{+0.15}_{-0.10}), the dynamical mass may be assumed to reflect the total baryonic mass, which can be used to obtain an estimate of MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} after subtracting MstarsM_{\rm stars}. Out of the 18 ALPINE non-merger galaxies with size measurements, for one galaxy55 5 In VUDS COSMOS 5101218326 the virial mass is smaller than MstarsM_{\rm stars}, likely because of an overestimation of MstarsM_{\rm stars} given the distorted morphology of the galaxy in the Hubble Space Telescope optical bands (Faisst et al., 2020), although we cannot exclude an underestimation of its virial mass as well. the virial mass ends up to be smaller than its MstarsM_{\rm stars}. For the remaining 17 ALPINE galaxies, we can cross-match the molecular gas masses obtained from their dynamical and stellar masses with the gas masses inferred from their [C ii] luminosity. For 12 ALPINE galaxies we consider the virial masses, and for the 5 ALPINE galaxies classified as rotation-dominated we consider the dynamical masses derived for a disk-like gas potential. As shown in Fig. 4, there is a good agreement within the 1​σ1\,\sigma uncertainty of 0.3 dex between these respective molecular gas mass estimates, except for two outliers (they do not show any systematic trend). A good one-to-one relationship between the two molecular gas mass estimates was expected, since the dynamical mass, if tracing the baryonic mass only (no dark matter), accounts for MstarsM_{\rm stars} plus the total gas mass that includes all gas phases (molecular, atomic, ionised) as likely does the [C ii] emission.

4 Comparison sample

Tremendous observational efforts have been dedicated to determine the molecular gas content of galaxies from the present day to high redshift, using either the CO emission or the FIR dust continuum as molecular gas mass tracers. These tracers have their respective strengths and uncertainties (Bolatto et al., 2013; Genzel et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2016; Tacconi et al., 2018, see). While the former tracer is the most commonly used and well-calibrated tracer in the local Universe, the latter tracer, which usually relies on a single-band measurement preferably in the Rayleigh-Jeans tail of the FIR SED, is particularly cheap in terms of ALMA observing time. Here we propose to compare the ALPINE MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} with a compilation of local to high-redshift MS SFGs with molecular gas masses derived from CO luminosity measurements reported in the literature.

We build up the database of CO-detected MS SFGs starting from the exhaustive compilation of CO luminosity measurements in MS SFGs at z>1z>1 presented in Dessauges-Zavadsky et al. (2015); Dessauges-Zavadsky et al. (2017). We extend this compilation with CO measurements at z>1z>1 published since 201566 6 We do not include the CO detection of D’Odorico et al. (2018) in our compilation of CO-detected MS SFGs, because MstarsM_{\rm stars} of the corresponding galaxy is not known. by Seko et al. (2016), Papovich et al. (2016), González-López et al. (2017), Magdis et al. (2017), Valentino et al. (2018), Gowardhan et al. (2019), Kaasinen et al. (2019), Molina et al. (2019), Aravena et al. (2019), Bourne et al. (2019), Pavesi et al. (2019), and Cassata et al. (2020). And we include the release of the NOEMA PHIBSS2 legacy survey at 0.5<z<2.50.5<z<2.5, described in Tacconi et al. (2018) and Freundlich et al. (2019). We adopt the MS parametrization from Speagle et al. (2014, Eq. (28)), similarly to what was done for PHIBSS2, and retain only SFGs lying within the MS dispersion of Δ​MS=log⁡(SFR/SFRMS)=±0.3\Delta{\rm MS}=\log({\rm SFR/SFR_{MS}})=\pm 0.3 dex. The updated compilation comprises a total of 101 CO luminosity measurements of MS SFGs at 1<z<3.71<z<3.7 and with Mstars=109.5−1011.7​M⊙M_{\rm stars}=10^{9.5}-10^{11.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}, plus the CO detection at z=5.65z=5.65 from Pavesi et al. The compilation of Dessauges-Zavadsky et al. (2015) also contained CO(1–0) measurements for a non-exhaustive number of local spiral galaxies and MS SFGs at z<1z<1. We now add the CO(1–0) measurements from the final xCOLD GASS survey at 0.01<z<0.050.01<z<0.05 performed with the IRAM 30 m telescope (Saintonge et al., 2016; Saintonge et al., 2017), which now extends to lower MstarsM_{\rm stars} than in previous samples, i.e. log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)=9−10\log(M_{\rm stars}/M_{\odot})=9-10.
