Finally, to check if our compilation of high-redshift SFGs at 0.1<z<3.70.1<z<3.7 with molecular gas masses derived from CO luminosity measurements is representative of MS SFGs at these redshifts, we consider the mean MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} obtained by Béthermin et al. (2015) from their stacking analysis of the IR to millimeter emission of MS SFGs, with an average MstarsM_{\rm stars} of ∼1010.8​M⊙\sim 10^{10.8}\penalty\ M_{\odot}, blindly selected in the COSMOS field between z=0.25z=0.25 and z=4z=4. For a coherent comparison, we rescale the molecular gas masses of Béthermin et al. (2015) to the mass-metallicity relation used in the CO compilation (Eq. (6)). Nevertheless, we keep the metallicity correction of 0.3×(1.7−z)0.3\times(1.7-z) dex they applied at z>1.7z>1.7 and which becomes significant for galaxies beyond z>2.5z>2.5. We find that the respective molecular gas depletion timescales and gas fractions globally agree, supporting that the sample of CO-detected SFGs is unbiased, except maybe in the redshift bin of 1<z<1.51<z<1.5 where the CO-measured molecular gas masses tend to be higher than the Béthermin et al. (2015) FIR SED stack results (see Fig. 6, left panel and Fig. 8, top panel).

Recently, Liu et al. (2019b) published MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} measurements for about 700 galaxies at 0.3<z<60.3<z<6, extracted on an automated prior-based and blind-based ALMA Archive mining in the COSMOS field (hereafter A3COSMOS, with spectroscopic redshifts available for 36% of the sample (Liu et al. 2019a)). The molecular gas masses were derived from single-band FIR continuum and multi-wavelength FIR SEDs. The A3COSMOS galaxies, however, are mostly probing the high MstarsM_{\rm stars} domain of MS SFGs at z>1z>1 with Mstars∼1011−1012​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\sim 10^{11}-10^{12}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. They thus are, on average, 10−10010-100 times more massive than the ALPINE [C ii]-detected galaxies that have a median MstarsM_{\rm stars} of ∼109.7​M⊙\sim 10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot} (and a mean of ∼1010​M⊙\sim 10^{10}\penalty\ M_{\odot}). Consequently, in terms of the respective MstarsM_{\rm stars} distributions shown in Fig. 5, our compilation of CO-detected MS galaxies at z>1z>1 represents a better comparison sample for the ALPINE galaxies, despite the fact that in the redshift range of ALPINE galaxies (z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9) one single CO detection is included, against 24 MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} measurements for MS SFGs in the A3COSMOS sample. With a median MstarsM_{\rm stars} of ∼1010.9​M⊙\sim 10^{10.9}\penalty\ M_{\odot} (and a mean of ∼1011​M⊙\sim 10^{11}\penalty\ M_{\odot}), the CO-detected SFGs globally have adequate masses at 1<z<3.71<z<3.7 to plausibly be the descendants of the ALPINE galaxies according to the multi-epoch abundance matching simulations (Behroozi et al., 2013; Behroozi et al., 2019; Moster et al., 2013; Moster et al., 2018), as discussed in Sect. 5.3.

5 Analysis and discussion

The comparison of the molecular gas masses inferred from the [C ii] luminosity, following the calibration proposed by Zanella et al. (2018), with three independent gas mass tracers discussed in Sect. 3.2 yields reassuring results supporting [C ii] as a statistically reliable tracer of cold molecular gas for the ALPINE galaxies. The [C ii]-estimated gas masses are associated with large error bars (∼0.3\sim 0.3 dex), but these error bars appear to be comparable to those of other tracers. In what follows, we adopt the [C ii] gas masses derived for the ALPINE galaxies to study the evolution of the molecular gas content of MS SFGs up to z∼6z\sim 6. We stress that if instead we choose another of the tested molecular gas mass tracers, we would obtain similar conclusions.

5.1 Molecular gas depletion timescale

From estimates of MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} and SFR of galaxies, we can infer their molecular gas depletion timescale, defined as tdepl=Mmolgas/SFRt_{\rm depl}=M_{\rm molgas}/{\rm SFR}. This gas depletion timescale (or gas consumption timescale) describes how long each galaxy may sustain star formation at the measured rate before running out of molecular gas fuel under the assumption that the gas reservoir is not replenished. Since the earliest CO luminosity measurements in high-redshift MS SFGs, there has been evidence for shorter tdeplt_{\rm depl} at high redshift, such that tdepl∼1−2t_{\rm depl}\sim 1-2 Gyr observed at z=0z=0 (Bigiel et al., 2008; Leroy et al., 2013; Saintonge et al., 2017, e.g.,) drops by a factor of ∼2\sim 2 at z∼2.5z\sim 2.5 (Tacconi et al., 2013; Tacconi et al., 2018; Tacconi et al., 2020; Saintonge et al., 2013; Genzel et al., 2015; Béthermin et al., 2015; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2017; Schinnerer et al., 2016; Scoville et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2019b, e.g.,). Shorter tdeplt_{\rm depl} correspond to higher star formation efficiencies (SFE=1/tdepl{\rm SFE}=1/t_{\rm depl}) that are taking place in high-redshift galaxies, efficient enough to exhaust similar and even larger gas reservoirs over a shorter timescale than in nearby MS SFGs. The so-far inferred tdeplt_{\rm depl} evolution with redshift, up to z∼3.5z\sim 3.5, nevertheless appears much shallower than tdepl∼(1+z)−1.5t_{\rm depl}\sim(1+z)^{-1.5} (see Fig. 6, left panel) that is predicted by semi-analytical and cosmological simulations developed in the framework of the bathtub model (Davé et al., 2011; Davé et al., 2012; Genel et al., 2014; Lagos et al., 2015, e.g.). This suggests that distant galaxies either intrinsically do not have such high SFE, or are more gas-rich than predicted, or outflows, if highly mass loaded, contribute to reduce the gas.

The ALPINE sample enables us, for the first time, to explore the tdeplt_{\rm depl} evolution beyond z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5 for a statistically significant number of MS SFGs with a median MstarsM_{\rm stars} of 109.7​M⊙10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. The measured tdeplt_{\rm depl} means and errors in two redshifts bins of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 are listed in Table 1. We provide both the means obtained when considering only the 44 [C ii]-detected galaxies and when also taking into account the “secure” 3​σ3\,\sigma upper limits of the 43 galaxies undetected in [C ii] (see Sect. 2). The latter means are computed using the survival analysis (Isobe et al., 1986, with routines described in). In particular, we use the Kaplan-Meier estimator, an unbiased non-parametric maximum likelihood estimator that determines the characteristic of a parent population with no assumption on the distribution of the parent population from which the censored sample is drawn (Talia et al., 2020, see also). The respective tdeplt_{\rm depl} means without/with limits differ by about a factor of 2.

In Fig. 6 (left panel) we show the molecular gas depletion timescale as a function of redshift for the ALPINE [C ii]-detected non-merger galaxies (red circles) and [C ii]-non-detected galaxies (light-red arrows) distributed in the redshift bins of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9, and for our compilation of CO-detected MS SFGs from the literature separated in 6 redshift bins of z=0z=0, 0<z<0.10<z<0.1, 0.1<z<10.1<z<1, 1<z<1.51<z<1.5, 1.5<z<2.51.5<z<2.5, and 2.5<z<3.72.5<z<3.7, chosen in the way that the three bins between z=0.1z=0.1 and z=2.5z=2.5 contain a comparable number of galaxies (∼40\sim 40). We then compute the respective means, errors on the mean, and standard deviations per redshift bin (black/grey big crosses). We show the ALPINE means obtained for the 44 [C ii] detections (see Table 1). We also overplot the depletion timescales obtained by Béthermin et al. (2015) from FIR SED stacks (light-grey shaded area). We observe a continuous decline of tdeplt_{\rm depl} from z=0z=0 to z=5.9z=5.9. The decline follows a power-law with a slope clearly shallower than (1+z)−1.5(1+z)^{-1.5} (dotted line), as this latter would imply tdepl=6.0×107t_{\rm depl}=6.0\times 10^{7} yr at z=5.5z=5.5 when fixing the zero-point at z=0z=0 to 1 Gyr. This predicted tdeplt_{\rm depl} value is comparable to the smallest ALPINE tdeplt_{\rm depl} measurement, but is almost one order of magnitude shorter than the mean tdeplt_{\rm depl} of (4.6±0.8)×108(4.6\pm 0.8)\times 10^{8} yr of the ALPINE [C ii]-detected non-merger galaxies in the redshift bin of 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9. Even if, for the ALPINE galaxies undetected in the FIR continuum emission, we add to their measured SFRUV\rm SFR_{UV} the possible SFRIR\rm SFR_{IR} contribution, estimated using the ALPINE IRX-β\beta relation obtained from stacking (Fudamoto et al., 2020) as discussed in Sect. 2, the resulting mean tdeplt_{\rm depl} of ∼3.8×108\sim 3.8\times 10^{8} yr over 4.4<z<5.94.4<z<5.9 is still too long compared to the (1+z)−1.5(1+z)^{-1.5} decline. When taking into account the “secure” 3​σ3\,\sigma upper limits of the ALPINE galaxies undetected in [C ii], the mean tdeplt_{\rm depl} drops to (2.3±0.4)×108(2.3\pm 0.4)\times 10^{8} yr in the redshift bin of 5.1 < z < 5.9. This drop suggests a steeper tdeplt_{\rm depl} decrease with redshift than shown by [C ii] detections, but the reached mean tdeplt_{\rm depl} value is still a factor of ∼4\sim 4 longer than for the predicted one. Consequently, on average, MS SFGs at z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5 are not considerably more efficient in forming stars than those galaxies at z∼2−3z\sim 2-3, as also supported by the low SFE obtained by Pavesi et al. (2019) from the CO(2–1) molecular gas mass measurement in a MS SFG at z=5.65z=5.65 (see the blue triangle at z=5.65z=5.65 in the left panel of Fig. 6).

There is a significant scatter, larger than 1 dex, among the tdeplt_{\rm depl} measurements in all redshift bins, even though we only consider MS galaxies with Δ​MS=±0.3\Delta{\rm MS}=\pm 0.3 dex around the MS parametrization of Speagle et al. (2014). This scatter at a fixed redshift is believed to be a product of the multi-functional dependence of tdeplt_{\rm depl} on many physical parameters, such as the offset from the MS, the star formation rate, the stellar mass, and possibly the environment (Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2017; Noble et al., 2017; Silverman et al., 2018; Tacconi et al., 2018; Tadaki et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2019b, e.g.,). Given the strong anti-correlation found between tdeplt_{\rm depl} and the offset from the MS (Genzel et al., 2015; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Tacconi et al., 2018), we still expect tdeplt_{\rm depl} variations for galaxies on the MS while in their evolutionary process they are transiting up and down across the MS band (Sargent et al., 2014; Tacchella et al., 2016, e.g.,). The previously reported anti-correlation between tdeplt_{\rm depl} and sSFR (Saintonge et al., 2011; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015) is also further supported by our galaxies at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 (Fig. 6, middle panel). It highlights comparable timescales for gas consumption and stellar mass formation (Saintonge et al., 2011; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015). We find a Spearman rank coefficient of −0.49-0.49 and pp-value of 4.5×10−104.5\times 10^{-10} for the dependence of tdeplt_{\rm depl} on sSFR when considering the MS SFGs at z∼1−5.9z\sim 1-5.9. The observed offset of ALPINE galaxies with respect to the tdeplt_{\rm depl}–sSFR relation of MS SFGs at z=0z=0 and to a lesser extent to the relations at z∼1z\sim 1 and z∼2z\sim 2 agrees with the displacement of the z=0z=0 relation along the sSFR-axis by factors derived from the redshift evolution of sSFR of MS SFGs out to redshifts of z∼5z\sim 5 (Speagle et al., 2014), although a less steep sSFR redshift evolution toward z∼5z\sim 5 than parametrised by Speagle et al. (2014) is suggested in line with the sSFR⁡(z){\rm sSFR}(z) results of Khusanova et al. (2020b). With tdeplt_{\rm depl} measurements achieved down to Mstars∼108.4​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\sim 10^{8.4}\penalty\ M_{\odot} for the ALPINE galaxies, we confirm, on the other hand, that for MS SFGs at z∼1−5.9z\sim 1-5.9 the tdeplt_{\rm depl} dependence on MstarsM_{\rm stars}, if any, must be weak as shown in Fig. 6 (right panel). This supports that the linear Kennicutt-Schmidt relation established for local galaxies (Kennicutt, 1998a) might hold up to z∼5.9z\sim 5.9 MS SFGs.

Scoville et al. (2017), Tacconi et al. (2018), and Liu et al. (2019b) performed, for their respective compilations of galaxies with MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} measurements, a multi-functional fitting to simultaneously quantify the underlying dependency of tdeplt_{\rm depl} as products of power laws in redshift, MstarsM_{\rm stars}, and offset from the MS (as well as optical size in the case of Tacconi et al. (2018), who ultimately found a negligible tdeplt_{\rm depl} dependence on size). They used slightly different criteria in their fitting procedure, but assumed the same MS parametrization from Speagle et al. (2014, Eq. (28))99 9 To be exact, Scoville et al. (2017) used a combination of MS parametrizations from Speagle et al. (2014) and Lee et al. (2015), but this combination only affects SFGs with high Mstars≳1010.5​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\gtrsim 10^{10.5}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. Below this mass threshold, the Speagle et al. (2014) MS parametrization holds.. Their respective best-fits yield different tdeplt_{\rm depl} functional forms, which are compared in Liu et al. (2019b). While the Tacconi et al. (2018) tdeplt_{\rm depl} function was fitted with data covering only redshifts of z∼0−3z\sim 0-3, the Liu et al. (2019b) function does account for data at z>3z>3, but restricted to MS SFGs with high MstarsM_{\rm stars} (Mstars∼1011​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\sim 10^{11}\penalty\ M_{\odot}). The three fitted functions in fact lack constraints for MS low mass (Mstars≲1010​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\lesssim 10^{10}\penalty\ M_{\odot}) SFGs at z>3z>3. These SFGs are particularly important, since, as shown by Liu et al. (2019b), the largest differences between the three fitted tdeplt_{\rm depl} functions are observed for MS SFGs at z>4z>4 with Mstars<1010​M⊙M_{\rm stars}<10^{10}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. The ALPINE galaxies are precisely characterised by these physical properties and can therefore bring decisive constraints on the tdeplt_{\rm depl} function.

In Fig. 7 (top panels) we show, similarly to Liu et al. (2019b), the molecular gas depletion timescale as a function of redshift as predicted by the three tdeplt_{\rm depl} best-fit functions for MS galaxies with Δ​MS\Delta{\rm MS} ranging from −0.3-0.3 dex to +0.3+0.3 dex and stellar masses in two bins of log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)=9.2−0.8+0.3\log(M_{\rm stars}/M_{\odot})=9.2^{+0.3}_{-0.8} and log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)=10−0.5+0.5\log(M_{\rm stars}/M_{\odot})=10^{+0.5}_{-0.5}. To compare the observations with the plotted best-fit functions, we bin the ALPINE galaxies in two redshift intervals of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 (red boxes), and the CO-detected MS SFGs from our compilation (Sect. 4) in three redshift intervals of 1<z<1.51<z<1.5, 1.5<z<2.51.5<z<2.5, and 2.5<z<3.72.5<z<3.7 (grey boxes). The blue boxes represent MS SFGs at 0<z<10<z<1 from A3COSMOS in Δ​z=0.3\Delta z=0.3 bins (Liu et al., 2019b). The ALPINE galaxies exclude the tdeplt_{\rm depl} best-fit function of Liu et al. (2019b) at z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5 in the two MstarsM_{\rm stars} bins, but already in the redshift bin of 2.5<z<3.72.5<z<3.7 we observe a deviation from this function in the log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)=10−0.5+0.5\log(M_{\rm stars}/M_{\odot})=10^{+0.5}_{-0.5} bin. On the other hand, both the Scoville et al. (2017) and Tacconi et al. (2018) tdeplt_{\rm depl} functions agree with the ALPINE observations, and this even if we consider the possible SFRIR\rm SFR_{IR} contribution for the ALPINE galaxies undetected in the FIR dust continuum (see Sect. 2), which would lower the plotted tdeplt_{\rm depl} means by a factor of 1.5 in the redshift bin of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and less in the higher redshift bin. The discrepancy of the Liu et al. (2019b) best-fit function with the other two functions results from the strong anti-correlation they find between tdeplt_{\rm depl} and MstarsM_{\rm stars}. This dependence of tdeplt_{\rm depl} on MstarsM_{\rm stars} is too strong for SFGs with Mstars<1010.5​M⊙M_{\rm stars}<10^{10.5}\penalty\ M_{\odot} at z≳3z\gtrsim 3, but seems to be correct at the high MstarsM_{\rm stars} end of Mstars≳1011​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\gtrsim 10^{11}\penalty\ M_{\odot} where both the Scoville et al. (2017) and Tacconi et al. (2018) functions overestimate the tdeplt_{\rm depl} measurements at z≳3z\gtrsim 3 (Liu et al., 2019b, see Fig. 12 in). We postpone the refitting of the functional form of tdeplt_{\rm depl} by including ALPINE galaxies in order to determine the scaling relation of tdeplt_{\rm depl} over a more complete MstarsM_{\rm stars} and redshift range to a future paper.

5.2 Molecular gas fraction

In Fig. 8 (top panel) we show the molecular gas fraction, defined as fmolgas=Mmolgas/(Mmolgas+Mstars)f_{\rm molgas}=M_{\rm molgas}/(M_{\rm molgas}+M_{\rm stars}), as a function of redshift for the ALPINE [C ii]-detected non-merger galaxies (red circles) and [C ii]-non-detected galaxies (light-red arrows) in the redshift bins of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9, and for our compilation of CO-detected MS SFGs from the literature separated in the same 6 redshift bins as in Sect. 5.1 and Fig. 6 of z=0z=0, 0<z<0.10<z<0.1, 0.1<z<10.1<z<1, 1<z<1.51<z<1.5, 1.5<z<2.51.5<z<2.5, and 2.5<z<3.72.5<z<3.7, chosen in the way that the three bins between z=0.1z=0.1 and z=2.5z=2.5 contain a comparable number of galaxies (about 40). We then compute the respective means, errors on the mean, and standard deviations per redshift bin (black/grey big crosses). We show the ALPINE means obtained for the 44 [C ii] detections (see Table 1). We also overplot the Béthermin et al. (2015) FIR SED stacks (light-grey shaded area). We observe a steep rise of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} from z=0z=0 to z∼3.7z\sim 3.7, in agreement with what has been previously reported (Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2017; Scoville et al., 2017; Tacconi et al., 2018; Tacconi et al., 2020, e.g.,). With the ALPINE sample we probe, for the first time, the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution beyond z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5 in MS SFGs with a low median MstarsM_{\rm stars} of 109.7​M⊙10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. Within the 1​σ1\,\sigma dispersion on the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} means in the two redshift bins, we observe a flattening of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} that reaches a mean value of 63%±3%63\%\pm 3\% over z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 (Table 1). The observed flattening is not subject to the assumptions that are needed to translate [C ii] luminosities into molecular gas masses, since both 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 redshift bins are subject to those assumptions in the same way. When applying the survival analysis to take into account the “secure” 3​σ3\,\sigma upper limits of the ALPINE galaxies undetected in [C ii] (Sect. 5.1), the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} means in the 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 redshift bins drop to 46%±5%46\%\pm 5\% (Table 1). This strengthens the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} flattening toward high redshifts, which is an important result, consistent with the evolutionary trend of a constant sSFR beyond z≳4z\gtrsim 4 obtained by several studies (Tasca et al., 2015; Khusanova et al., 2020a, e.g.,), including the sSFR derived from the obscured SFR measured in the ALPINE galaxies by stacking the FIR dust continuum maps in the redshift bins of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 (Khusanova et al., 2020b). The finding that fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} and sSFR merely have a similar evolution with redshift is not a surprise, since fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} can be expressed as a function of tdeplt_{\rm depl} and sSFR (Tacconi et al., 2013):

fmolgas=11+(sSFR​tdepl)−1.f_{\rm molgas}=\frac{1}{1+({\rm sSFR}\penalty\ t_{\rm depl})^{-1}}. (7)

As a result, the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} redshift evolution depends on the redshift evolution of both tdeplt_{\rm depl} and sSFR. In the case of, on average, a weak change in tdeplt_{\rm depl} of MS SFGs with redshift, which is what we observe in Fig. 6 (left panel), we globally have fmolgas​(z)∝sSFR⁡(z)f_{\rm molgas}(z)\propto{\rm sSFR}(z).

In the framework of the bathtub model, the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution with redshift reflects an interplay between cosmic inflow (supply of fresh gas onto galaxies) and gas consumption rates, modulo outflows. The mass accretion rate was shown to scale as (1+z)2.25(1+z)^{2.25} (Dekel et al., 2009), therefore the gas supply rate drops faster with time than the gas consumption rate (see Sect. 5.1). This explains why galaxies at sufficiently high redshifts begin to be gas-rich, but then fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} drops as the gas consumption rate catches up. The phase during which galaxies have an excess of gas, and hence are in non-equilibrium, will also depend on feedback, since outflows, by ejecting the gas out of galaxies, reduce the amount of gas that needs to be processed into stars and help to establish the equilibrium earlier on. A quick look at the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} observations supports a gas excess until at most z∼3z\sim 3 (Fig. 8, top panel). This is much shorter in cosmic time than predicted by cosmological simulations of Lagos et al. (2015), who report a drop of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} only several Gyr later, by z∼1z\sim 1. Given the shallow tdeplt_{\rm depl} evolution with redshift, outflows must play an important role in blowing out part of the infalling gas at z≳3z\gtrsim 3. This is supported by signatures of star formation-driven outflows in stacks of [C ii] spectra and [C ii] moment-zero maps and stacks of rest-frame UV spectra of the ALPINE higher SFR (≳25​M⊙\gtrsim 25\penalty\ M_{\odot} yr-1) galaxies (Ginolfi et al., 2020a; Faisst et al., 2020), but also observed in a few individual ALPINE objects with [C ii] halos (Fujimoto et al., 2020; Ginolfi et al., 2020b). Observational evidence of star formation-driven outflows in SFGs at z≲5−6z\lesssim 5-6 was also reported in other studies (Sugahara et al., 2019; Rubin et al., 2014; Talia et al., 2017, e.g.,).

While we observe an overall flattening of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} toward high redshifts, some individual galaxies appear to depart from this average trend considerably: the scatter in fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} among ALPINE MS SFGs ranges from ∼15\sim 15% to ∼95\sim 95%. A significant scatter among fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} measurements is observed in all redshift bins (although the scatter is particularly large at 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9). The tight correlation between fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} and offset from the MS, reported even for MS SFGs lying within the ±0.3\pm 0.3 dex dispersion of the MS (Tacconi et al., 2013; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Genzel et al., 2015; Saintonge et al., 2016), certainly contributes to this fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} scatter per redshift bin. In addition to that, there is a strong dependence of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} on MstarsM_{\rm stars} as shown in the bottom panel of Fig. 8, previously found for local and z≲3z\lesssim 3 MS SFGs (Saintonge et al., 2011; Tacconi et al., 2013; Tacconi et al., 2018; Tacconi et al., 2020; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Schinnerer et al., 2016; Scoville et al., 2017, e.g.,), and now assessed for the ALPINE z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 galaxies (Spearman rank coefficient of −0.50-0.50 and pp-value of 7.0×10−47.0\times 10^{-4}). The observed steep drop in fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} with increasing MstarsM_{\rm stars} is expected from the gas conversion into stars, and is predicted by semi-analytical simulations developed in the framework of the bathtub model, as well as cosmological hydrodynamic simulations, for both local and high-redshift galaxies (Bouché et al., 2010; Davé et al., 2011; Davé et al., 2017). This behaviour was proposed to be consistent with the “downsizing” scenario, where at fixed redshift massive galaxies have lower fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} because they consumed their fuel of star formation earlier than less massive galaxies that still have large fractions of gas (Bouché et al., 2010; Santini et al., 2014; Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Scoville et al., 2017). We find that the significant fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} scatter of ALPINE galaxies must be mostly driven by the large range of MstarsM_{\rm stars}, from 108.4​M⊙10^{8.4}\penalty\ M_{\odot} to 1011​M⊙10^{11}\penalty\ M_{\odot}, they encompass.

Similarly to the multi-functional fitting performed by Scoville et al. (2017), Tacconi et al. (2018), and Liu et al. (2019b) for tdeplt_{\rm depl}, we show in the bottom panels of Fig. 7 the best-fit functions obtained for the molecular gas ratio, μmolgas=Mmolgas/Mstars\mu_{\rm molgas}=M_{\rm molgas}/M_{\rm stars}, as a function of redshift for MS galaxies with Δ​MS\Delta{\rm MS} ranging from −0.3-0.3 dex to +0.3+0.3 dex and stellar masses in two bins of log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)=9.2−0.8+0.3\log(M_{\rm stars}/M_{\odot})=9.2^{+0.3}_{-0.8} and log⁡(Mstars/M⊙)=10−0.5+0.5\log(M_{\rm stars}/M_{\odot})=10^{+0.5}_{-0.5}. We consider these two MstarsM_{\rm stars} bins, because it is at these MstarsM_{\rm stars} that the larger differences between the three fitted μmolgas\mu_{\rm molgas} functions are found. To compare the observations with the plotted best-fit functions, we bin again the ALPINE galaxies in two redshift intervals of 4.4<z<4.64.4<z<4.6 and 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 (red boxes), and the CO-detected MS SFGs from our compilation (Sect. 4) in three redshift intervals of 1<z<1.51<z<1.5, 1.5<z<2.51.5<z<2.5, and 2.5<z<3.72.5<z<3.7 (grey boxes). The blue boxes represent MS SFGs at 0<z<10<z<1 from A3COSMOS in Δ​z=0.3\Delta z=0.3 bins (Liu et al., 2019b). Our data favour the Tacconi et al. (2018) best-fit function, given the comparable decrease of the predicted and measured μmolgas\mu_{\rm molgas} at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9, and the tdeplt_{\rm depl} results discussed in Sect. 5.1. This function also provides a good fit to the μmolgas\mu_{\rm molgas} redshift evolution of massive MS SFGs (Liu et al., 2019b, see Fig. 13 in). On the other hand, the Scoville et al. (2017) function overestimates the molecular gas ratios of MS SFGs in both MstarsM_{\rm stars} bins considered.

5.3 Molecular gas fraction over cosmic time

As stressed by Wiklind et al. (2019), to probe the true evolution of galaxy properties over cosmic time, galaxies need to be carefully selected in a way which correctly connects the progenitors at high redshifts with their descendants at z=0z=0. A possible selection method is to use the multi-epoch abundance matching, which links as a function of redshift the growth of central dark matter halos, as derived from numerical simulations, with the growth of stellar content constrained from observations of the MstarsM_{\rm stars} function (Behroozi et al., 2013; Behroozi et al., 2019; Moster et al., 2013; Moster et al., 2018). The redshift evolution of the resulting stellar-to-halo mass relation is driven by gas accretion, star formation, feedback (leading to stellar mass loss), and eventually merging processes.

Following the work by Behroozi et al. (2019, top right panel of Fig. 18), we use the evolutionary corridors they computed, in the MstarsM_{\rm stars} versus redshift plane, for the stellar mass histories of progenitors of z=0z=0 galaxies with a given MstarsM_{\rm stars} range. The ALPINE [C ii]-detected non-merger galaxies with their MstarsM_{\rm stars} appear to be the progenitors, at z∼4.5z\sim 4.5 and z∼5.5z\sim 5.5, of Milky Way-like galaxies at z=0z=0 with MstarsM_{\rm stars} in the range of ∼1010.8​M⊙\sim 10^{10.8}\penalty\ M_{\odot} and 1011.2​M⊙10^{11.2}\penalty\ M_{\odot} and of more massive z=0z=0 galaxies with Mstars∼1011.4−1011.7​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\sim 10^{11.4}-10^{11.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. The range of MstarsM_{\rm stars} of these z=0z=0 descendants with halo masses of Mhalo=1013​M⊙M_{\rm halo}=10^{13}\penalty\ M_{\odot} and 1014​M⊙10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} at z=0z=0, respectively, were carefully chosen such that their respective stellar mass histories do not overlap in the MstarsM_{\rm stars}–zz plane. In Table 2 we list the respective stellar mass histories. We then select, in our compilation of CO-detected MS SFGs and ALPINE galaxies, progenitors with the specific MstarsM_{\rm stars} over cosmic time from z>0z>0 to z=5.9z=5.9.

As shown in Fig. 9, we find a different evolution of the molecular gas fraction from z=5.9z=5.9 to the present day for progenitors of Milky Way-analogues and for more massive z=0z=0 galaxies. Progenitors of Milky Way-like galaxies follow a monotonic decrease of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} with cosmic time, which steepens at z≲1z\lesssim 1. However, this result relies on only three ALPINE fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} measurements in the redshift bin of 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9, which show galaxies dominated by gas with a mean fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} as high as 90%±4%90\%\pm 4\%. A larger sample of low MstarsM_{\rm stars} galaxies in this redshift bin is necessary to confirm the currently observed monotonic decrease. Progenitors of the more massive z=0z=0 galaxies show, on the other hand, a steep fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} decline at z≲2z\lesssim 2, which is preceded by a flat fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution at higher redshifts, with a mean value of 63%±3%63\%\pm 3\% at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9, although some hint of an fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} rise from z∼5.5z\sim 5.5 to z∼4.5z\sim 4.5 exits. How can we explain these different fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolutions with cosmic time?

As discussed in Sect. 5.2, galaxies are believed to be supplied with cold gas by cosmic accretion flows. This accreted gas can then be used for the MstarsM_{\rm stars} build-up of galaxies, if not partly expelled by outflows from the galaxy. Ginolfi et al. (2020a) showed evidence of star formation-driven outflows in the [C ii] emission stacks of the ALPINE galaxies with SFR higher than the median SFR of the APLINE sample (SFR>25​M⊙​yr−1{\rm SFR}>25\penalty\ M_{\odot}\penalty\ \rm yr^{-1}). These higher SFR galaxies are also the more massive ones, due to their placement on the MS (Faisst et al., 2020). As a result, the observed outflows could contribute more to moderate the gas content available for star formation in the massive ALPINE galaxies, progenitors of 1014​M⊙10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} halo mass galaxies at z=0z=0, and could explain their flat fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution from z=5.9z=5.9 to z=4.4z=4.4 (Fig. 9, right panel) given also the induced quenching of star formation yielding a temporarily decrease of the gas consumption rate. This scenario matches with the non-detection of star formation-driven outflows in the less star-forming (and therefore, on average, less massive) ALPINE galaxies (Ginolfi et al., 2020a), progenitors at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 of Milky Way-like galaxies, and hence with the observed steady decrease of their fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} from z=5.9z=5.9 to z=4.4z=4.4 (Fig. 9, left panel).

Moreover, it has also been suggested by simulations that for very massive dark matter halos the gas supply starts to shut off and prevents star formation (Dekel & Birnboim, 2006; Keres̆ et al., 2009; Bouché et al., 2010). This is due to the fact that as the halo grows larger, it reaches the threshold for virial shock heating (Mshock≲1012​M⊙M_{\rm shock}\lesssim 10^{12}\penalty\ M_{\odot}) and, consequently, the infalling cold gas shock heats up close to the virial temperature (Dekel et al., 2009). Our data suggest that this might be happening at z∼5z\sim 5 in ∼1011.5−11.8​M⊙\sim 10^{11.5-11.8}\penalty\ M_{\odot} halos, the progenitors of z=0z=0 halos of 1014​M⊙10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} (see Fig. 9, right panel). This indirectly implies that these massive galaxies must be mature by z∼5z\sim 5 and probably quench earlier than lower mass galaxies. Comparing right and left panels of Fig. 9, we observe that the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} means of massive galaxies are smaller by ∼10\sim 10% (on absolute scale) in the redshift bins of 1<z<1.51<z<1.5 and 0.1<z<10.1<z<1 than those of lower mass galaxies.

On the other hand, massive progenitors have to grow a lot in the past to build up their large MstarsM_{\rm stars}. But, is there still enough cold gas for them to grow sufficiently quickly to reach these MstarsM_{\rm stars} by z∼5z\sim 5, if we advocate that the cold gas accreted on galaxies is either removed by outflows or reduced because of the suppression of the cosmic accretion flows? The constant fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} observed between z=5.9z=5.9 and z=4.4z=4.4, with even a possibly lower fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} value in the 5.1<z<5.95.1<z<5.9 redshift bin, may also be the result of an efficient star formation in these massive SFGs, such that the infalling gas is rapidly converted into stars. Some evidence for a higher SFE in massive ALPINE galaxies is shown in Fig. 6 (right panel), where, when considering the ALPINE galaxies only, we see a trend for an anti-correlation between tdeplt_{\rm depl} and MstarsM_{\rm stars} (Spearman rank coefficient of −0.33-0.33 and pp-value of 0.0016). Liu et al. (2019b) reported such an anti-correlation, but for the whole sample of SFGs from z∼6z\sim 6 to z=0z=0. We find, on the contrary, that this anti-correlation is not present for MS SFGs at z≲3.7z\lesssim 3.7 (Dessauges-Zavadsky et al., 2015; Tacconi et al., 2018, see also). We rather argue that the tdeplt_{\rm depl} dependence on MstarsM_{\rm stars} might change across the cosmic time, from a negative slope at high redshift to the positive slope that is observed for local galaxies (Saintonge et al., 2017, e.g.,).

6 Summary and conclusions

We use observations from the ALPINE [C ii] 158 μ\mum survey of UV-selected star-forming galaxies at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 (Le Fèvre et al., 2020; Faisst et al., 2020; Béthermin et al., 2020) and the correlation between [C ii] luminosity and molecular gas mass recently proposed by Zanella et al. (2018), to obtain MmolgasCIIM^{\rm CII}_{\rm molgas} estimates of 44 [C ii]-detected MS SFGs with a median MstarsM_{\rm stars} of 109.7​M⊙10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot} (Fig. 1). Prior our work, measurements of MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} at z>4z>4 have been derived for 24 MS SFGs from A3COSMOS based on the thermal dust FIR continuum emission (Liu et al., 2019b), all having MstarsM_{\rm stars} one order of magnitude larger than those of ALPINE galaxies. And only two CO-derived molecular gas masses have been reported in MS SFGs at z>5z>5 (Pavesi et al., 2019; D’Odorico et al., 2018).

The [C ii] luminosity appears to be an effective tracer of the gas mass of ALPINE galaxies with a 1​σ1\,\sigma uncertainty of 0.30.3 dex. This level of error is assessed by comparing molecular gas mass estimates based on [C ii] luminosity, rest-frame 158 μ\mum continuum emission (measured for 11 galaxies; Fig. 3), and dynamical mass (determined for 17 galaxies with size measurements; Fig. 4). The agreement with the dynamical mass, essentially probing the baryonic gas mass after removing MstarsM_{\rm stars} (the relative dark matter contribution in the internal regions of galaxies is expected to be low), supports that LCIIL_{\rm CII} likely traces the total gas mass including the molecular, atomic, and ionised gas phases, and hence possibly overestimates the true MmolgasM_{\rm molgas} unless the atomic and ionised gas masses are negligible as often assumed at high redshift.

Accurate MstarsM_{\rm stars} and SFR were obtained for the ALPINE galaxies from existing ancillary UV to IR data (Faisst et al., 2020). Together with MmolgasM_{\rm molgas}, we derive fundamental physical quantities, which are the molecular gas depletion timescale and the molecular gas fraction, and explore scaling-relations between these physical quantities. To put the ALPINE galaxies in a global context, we build a comparison sample of MS SFGs between z=0z=0 and z∼3.7z\sim 3.7 with molecular gas mass measurements inferred from CO luminosities reported in the literature. Our main results can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    The ALPINE sample enables us to explore the tdeplt_{\rm depl} evolution beyond z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5 for a statistically significant number of MS SFGs. We observe a continuous decline of tdeplt_{\rm depl} from z=0z=0 to z∼5.9z\sim 5.9, reaching a mean value of (4.6±0.8)×108(4.6\pm 0.8)\times 10^{8} yr at z=5.1−5.9z=5.1-5.9, which confirms a tdeplt_{\rm depl} redshift evolution with a slope shallower than (1+z)−1.5(1+z)^{-1.5} that is predicted in the framework of the bathtub model (Fig. 6, left panel). This suggests that MS SFGs at z≳4.5z\gtrsim 4.5 are not considerably more efficient in forming stars, only a factor of 2−32-3 with respect to present-day galaxies, or undergo a significant increase in their fmolgasf_{\rm molgas}. The large tdeplt_{\rm depl} scatter of more than 1 dex per redshift bin is attributed to the multi-functional dependence of tdeplt_{\rm depl} on various physical parameters, such as their offset from the MS, star formation rate, and stellar mass. With the ALPINE galaxies probing low-to-moderate MstarsM_{\rm stars} with a median of 109.7​M⊙10^{9.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot}, we find that MS SFGs at z∼1−5.9z\sim 1-5.9 show no tdeplt_{\rm depl} dependence on MstarsM_{\rm stars} (Fig. 6, right panel).

  • •

    We confirm that the steep rise of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} is confined between z=0z=0 and z∼3.7z\sim 3.7. At higher redshift, as shown by ALPINE galaxies, the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution flattens and reaches a mean value as high as 63%±3%63\%\pm 3\% over z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 (Fig. 8, top panel). The fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} flattening is consistent with the sSFR redshift evolution, which also flattens beyond z≳4z\gtrsim 4 according to several studies, including the results on the obscured SFR measured in the ALPINE galaxies by stacking the FIR dust continuum maps (Khusanova et al., 2020b). The redshift, at which the turnover in the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution happens, depends on when the gas consumption rate catches up to the mass accretion rate. We observe a gas excess until at most z∼3z\sim 3, which, given the slow tdeplt_{\rm depl} evolution with redshift, suggests that outflows may play an important role in blowing out part of the infalling gas at z≳4z\gtrsim 4. We attribute the large scatter in fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} of ALPINE galaxies, from ∼10\sim 10% to ∼95\sim 95%, to mostly MstarsM_{\rm stars} (Fig. 8, lower panel), given the strong dependence of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} observed on MstarsM_{\rm stars} (Fig. 8, bottom panel) that reflects an important “downsizing” effect from massive to low-mass galaxies at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9.

  • •

    The [C ii]-detected ALPINE galaxies at z=4.4−5.9z=4.4-5.9 and the currently available compilation of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} measurements in CO-detected MS SFGs at z∼0−3.7z\sim 0-3.7 enables us, for the first time, to probe the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution over cosmic time, from z=5.9z=5.9 to the present day, of the progenitors of z=0z=0 Milky Way-like galaxies with MstarsM_{\rm stars} in the range of ∼1010.8−1011.2​M⊙\sim 10^{10.8}-10^{11.2}\penalty\ M_{\odot} for a halo mass of 1013​M⊙10^{13}\penalty\ M_{\odot} and of more massive z=0z=0 galaxies with Mstars∼1011.4−1011.7​M⊙M_{\rm stars}\sim 10^{11.4}-10^{11.7}\penalty\ M_{\odot} for a halo mass of 1014​M⊙10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot}. We use the multi-epoch abundance matching predictions of Behroozi et al. (2019) to select progenitors’ MstarsM_{\rm stars} as a function of redshift (Table 2). We observe a different redshift evolution of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} for the respective progenitors of galaxy halos of different masses (Fig. 9), where lower mass halos (Mhalo=1013​M⊙M_{\rm halo}=10^{13}\penalty\ M_{\odot} at z=0z=0) show a monotonic decrease of fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} with cosmic time and the higher mass halos (Mhalo=1014​M⊙M_{\rm halo}=10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} at z=0z=0) show, on average, a flat fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} until z∼2z\sim 2 followed by a steep decrease at z≲2z\lesssim 2. This difference, if confirmed, likely reveals important changes in the physical conditions of MS SFGs at z∼5z\sim 5 for a specific halo mass threshold. To explain the flat fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} evolution from z=5.9z=5.9 to z=4.4z=4.4 of progenitors of z=0z=0 halos with 1014​M⊙10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} masses, we discuss the effect of possibly stronger star formation-driven outflows in these more massive ALPINE galaxies as observed by Ginolfi et al. (2020a, and also , ), which could remove their accreted cold gas and temporarily quench star formation. Simulations also suggest that for very massive dark matter halos, the gas supply starts to shut off. According to the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} redshift evolution observed for the ALPINE galaxies, this seems to happen at z∼5z\sim 5 in halos of ∼1011.5−11.8​M⊙\sim 10^{11.5-11.8}\penalty\ M_{\odot}, progenitors of 1014​M⊙10^{14}\penalty\ M_{\odot} halos at z=0z=0. Alternatively, we argue for a possible evidence of a higher SFE in the more massive ALPINE galaxies that is also necessary for the quick stellar mass build-up of these galaxies. To conclude, certainly the three effects, namely outflows, halt of gas supplying, and over-efficient star formation, jointly contribute to the fmolgasf_{\rm molgas} plateau observed for the massive galaxies at =4.4−5.9=4.4-5.9.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
